title: Malicious prosecution requires wrongful institution or continuation of proceedings, favourable termination, absence of reasonable and probable cause, malice and actionable damage

content.overview: Malicious prosecution requires wrongful institution or continuation of proceedings, favourable termination, absence of reasonable and probable cause, malice and actionable damage. Abuse of process instead concerns misuse of lawful process for an improper collateral purpose.
content.glance: Malicious prosecution requires wrongful institution or continuation of proceedings, favourable termination, absence of reasonable and probable cause, malice and actionable damage. Abuse of process instead concerns misuse of lawful process for an improper collateral purpose.
content.study: Malicious prosecution requires wrongful institution or continuation of proceedings, favourable termination, absence of reasonable and probable cause, malice and actionable damage. Abuse of process instead concerns misuse of lawful process for an improper collateral purpose.\n\nThe tort balances access to justice against protection from baseless proceedings. Indian courts do not infer malice merely because a prior proceeding ended favourably. The cause of action ordinarily matures after favourable termination. Abuse of process focuses on collateral misuse rather than simply the merits of the original case.

sections.heading: Provenance, Legislative Objective & Doctrinal Foundations
sections.body: The tort balances access to justice against protection from baseless proceedings. Indian courts do not infer malice merely because a prior proceeding ended favourably. The cause of action ordinarily matures after favourable termination. Abuse of process focuses on collateral misuse rather than simply the merits of the original case.

sections.heading: Textual Anatomy, Provisos & Statutory Deconstruction
sections.body: There is no general statutory codification. The claimant must establish the common-law ingredients. A bona fide complaint based on reasonable information is not transformed into malicious prosecution by later acquittal alone.

sections.heading: Mandatory Proving Ingredients & Essential Elements
sections.body: 1. Defendant instituted or was instrumental in proceedings. 2. Proceedings terminated favourably. 3. No reasonable and probable cause. 4. Malice. 5. Legally recognised damage. Abuse of process requires proof of collateral misuse.

sections.heading: Evidentiary Burdens under BSA 2023 (ss. 104–106 & s. 63)
sections.body: Prior pleadings, complaint, investigation material, orders, acquittal or discharge and surrounding correspondence are central. Reasonable cause is assessed on information available when proceedings were initiated.

sections.heading: Procedural Roadmap, Competent Forum & Limitation Act Checkpoints
sections.body: The action ordinarily follows favourable termination. Plead each ingredient and specific facts showing malice and lack of reasonable cause. Limitation runs from the applicable accrual point.

examples.title: Illustration 1 — Doctrine Satisfied
examples.body: Favourable termination alone is insufficient; the other ingredients must be independently proved. The claimant must still prove the remaining ingredients on the civil standard.

examples.title: Illustration 2 — Boundary Defect
examples.body: The claimant must also prove absence of reasonable and probable cause, malice and actionable damage. A court should not infer liability from the label alone.

distinctions.title: Malicious prosecution vs Abuse of process
distinctions.right: Malicious prosecution concerns wrongful institution or continuation; abuse of process concerns collateral misuse of judicial process.

rows.left: Favourable termination alone is insufficient; the other ingredients must be independently proved.
rows.right: Malicious prosecution concerns wrongful institution or continuation; abuse of process concerns collateral misuse of judicial process.

rows.left: Apply the ingredients of the pleaded tort.
rows.right: Do not substitute the neighbouring cause of action.

misconceptions.trap: Acquittal automatically gives a tort claim
misconceptions.correction: The claimant must also prove absence of reasonable and probable cause, malice and actionable damage.
